transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-07
Start time: 16:00 PST
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (CTO - Crescent), Mark Holloway (SRE - Crescent), Elena Rossi (ML Eng - Crescent)

Summary:
Quick deep dive to understand observed latency delta when customers enable JSON-mode / strict structured output + function/tool calling. Focus on where time is spent in the runtime (tokenization, constraint checks, kernel IO, KV cache interactions, batching regime) and what to try on their on-prem stack.

Shared artifacts referenced: short-bench.csv (link shared in chat), redwood-json-mode-tuning.pdf (shared), onprem-network-topology.png (customer uploaded).

Topics: function calling overhead, constrained decoding path, KV hits/misses, batching policies, quantization trade-offs, VPC/netting issues.

[00:00] Maya: ok thanks everyone for joining, we wanted to run through the numbers you sent and talk through exactly where the extra latency is coming from when you enable json_mode and function calling constraints. quick intros?
[00:12] Priya: hi, priya here. we run Crescent's inference platform in our co-lo and are evaluating running critical inference behind our VPC. Mark and Elena are here to help with infra and model details.
[00:25] Mark: hey, quick note — latency targets are tight for us: p99 under 450ms for 512-token prompts. we saw p99 jump to ~820ms when we switched to strict-json outputs.
[00:36] Luis: important to know — is that p99 measured on your onprem with our dedicated runtime or a self-hosted baseline?
[00:44] Elena: that's on our onprem with your runtime image (we're using the v1.12 runtime build); we ran float16, no special quant, and enabled JSON-mode + function calls.
[00:56] Luis: ok. couple quick hypotheses: (1) constrained decoding adds per-token bookkeeping (token-level constraint checks), (2) KV cache miss pattern due to different session prefixing, and (3) batching policy causes head-of-line latency when continuous batching combines strict-decoding tokens. also quantization can shift kernel choices.
[01:14] Priya: can you explain the token-level overhead in plain terms? our infra folks think JSON-mode should be a small cost.
[01:20] Maya: sure — in JSON-mode we insert a token validator that checks allowed token sequences to enforce structural constraints; that validator runs synchronous checks per token and depending on implementation can cause a 1.1x-1.4x per-token time increase. it also prevents some decoding optimizations like very long beam-level shortcuts.
[01:38] Luis: yes, additionally when the validator signals disallowed tokens we may do extra reranking steps; on GPU that can mean extra kernels triggered rather than pure next-token softmax. in practice on an A100 we saw anywhere 8-20% extra wall-clock per token for strict JSON emulation. on older hardware or with int8 kernels the proportion can be different.
[01:59] Mark: is that consistent across sequence length? we saw latency blow up more at 512 vs 128 tokens.
[02:06] Luis: constrained checks are per token, so the total adds with length. but a second effect: for longer sequences the KV cache accesses cost more memory io, and if your KV cache isn't pinned or is paged due to memory pressure on the host that adds more non-linear latency.
[02:20] Elena: we did observe occasional spikes where CPU threads on the host were getting saturated — maybe mmap thrashing? our nodes have 256GB swap off, but still.
[02:30] Maya: that resonates — on-prem often has different NUMA and I/O characteristics. We also saw cases where VPC networking for private control-plane callbacks added 50-70ms when function invocation required a small sidecar call to a tool.
[02:45] Priya: wait, is the function call handled inside the same runtime or proxied externally? we thought it was internal.
[02:50] Luis: depends on config. simple tool calls that are handled by runtime-internal hooks are in-process, but many PII scrubbers or enterprise tools are proxied through a local microservice which adds network latency. in the customer setup you had a tool-proxy in front of your DLP service, so that path will add ~30-60ms per invocation.
[03:06] Mark: ok noted. can we focus on KV cache? our p95 goes down with cache warmup but p99 is still bad.
[03:12] Luis: two patterns: cache hit rates and cache fragmentation. if sessions use slightly different prefixes (timestamps, user ids embedded) your prefix cache hit rate drops. second, cache eviction. the runtime caches KV at chunk granularity; if your session uses long context mixing you may thrash small caches.
[03:27] Elena: we're using conversational style with user metadata in the prompt, so likely low hit rate. any ways to mitigate?
[03:33] Maya: best practices — canonicalize prompts (remove nonce fields), use a small hashed prefix mapping, and enable prefix-only caching mode for certain endpoints so the runtime only caches the model KV for the stable system instruction + last n tokens rather than entire raw prompt. we'll share a sample canonicalizer.
[03:47] Priya: you said earlier about batching causing head-of-line latency. can you elaborate?
[03:51] Luis: sure — our continuous batching groups requests within a short window to increase throughput. If JSON-mode requests are slower per-token, they hold the batch open longer which increases latency for faster requests in the same batch. Two levers: isolate strict-json endpoints into a dedicated pool (different batch policy) or use a small max-batch-size + tight batching window for latency-sensitive routes.
[04:10] Mark: could we just turn off batching for those endpoints?
[04:12] Luis: you can, but cost will rise. Dedicated pools let you trade cost for consistent latency. There's also 'progressive decode' which streams partial tokens back and lets the client stop early, but that interacts poorly with strict JSON validation because partial outputs may not be valid JSON.
[04:30] Elena: about quantization — we plan to move to int8 for cost. does quantization affect JSON-mode latency differently?
[04:35] Luis: yes — int8 kernels are highly optimized for throughput, but some constrained-decoding code paths (the validator, re-ranking) may not be vectorized for int8 and trigger FP16 fallbacks on critical sections. So you get mixed precision penalties. On some platforms we measured a 10-15% latency increase compared to float16 for the strict JSON path due to those fallbacks.
[04:56] Priya: wow — so int8 could save cost but worsen tail latency for structured output. Any recommended configs?
[05:02] Maya: common approach: run int8 for non-strict endpoints and keep float16 for strict-json routes, or tune quantization-aware kernels. Also attempt quantize-aware validator: pre-compile token masks in the same precision to avoid fallbacks. We'll provide a tuning guide.
[05:16] Mark: can caching be shared across precision variants? we saw a mismatch where warm cache under float16 doesn't help int8 runs.
[05:23] Luis: cache entries are precision-aware because KV blobs differ by kernel packing. You can enable a unified KV serialization format but that requires runtime conversion overhead. There's an experimental config where we keep a canonical float16 cache on disk and load/convert to int8 on warmup — helping cold-starts but adding conversion cost.
[05:40] Elena: let's talk benchmarks you ran — what numbers are typical?
[05:44] Luis: quick example from our lab on A100: baseline float16 no constraints: p95 210ms for 256 tokens. Enable JSON-mode strict validator -> p95 255ms, p99 climbs 280-320ms. On older V100-class hardware with int8, baseline 260ms -> JSON-mode p95 310-360ms and p99 higher. Those are ballpark; your onprem topology and proxy patterns can worsen things.
[06:09] Priya: your CSV shows a big delta at p99 when batch size increases — is that because of the batching window?
[06:16] Luis: yes, batch window plus slower token steps in constrained decode compound; also queueing on the CPU tokenizer thread can add jitter if tokenization is CPU-bound during high concurrency.
[06:29] Maya: we should inspect your tokenization pattern. are you using raw UTF-8 prompts with lots of emojis or non-ascii? that can increase tokenization time.
[06:36] Elena: mostly ascii, but we do include some short HTML snippets occasionally.
[06:40] Luis: html can increase token length due to tokenization subword splits; canonicalization helps.
[06:46] Mark: network impact — earlier you mentioned VPC sidecars adding latency for function calls. can we host the tool in process?
[06:53] Luis: yes — if the tool logic is safe to run inside the same process (no blocking IO, memory safe), you can register a local tool plugin. For enterprise security often teams prefer proxied services. If you keep it local you cut 30-70ms per call.
[07:06] Priya: is the function-call flow synchronous per token or batched?
[07:09] Luis: typically the function call is triggered when the model emits a special token sequence; it's synchronous with the decode loop (model pauses waiting for the tool). So any external call blocks decoding. That's why we recommend local plugin or async callback patterns where the runtime can speculatively continue alternative decoding paths (experimental).
[07:27] Maya: note — speculative decoding can blow up cost if you run multiple branches to hedge, so it's a tradeoff.
[07:33] Priya: makes sense. This is a lot. Can you summarize concrete mitigations for us to try this week?
[07:39] Luis: sure: (1) canonicalize prompts to improve KV hit rate, (2) isolate strict-json routes onto smaller-batch pools or dedicated nodes, (3) keep float16 for strict-json if p99 is critical or test int8 kernel builds that include validator optimizations, (4) host simple tools in-process to remove network hops, (5) share sample prompts so we can run microbench on your hardware.
[07:59] Mark: for the microbench, what config should we run?
[08:02] Luis: we'll send a script. Quick checklist: run float16 baseline, float16+json-mode, int8 baseline, int8+json-mode; for each measure p50/p95/p99 and throughput; include cold and warm cache runs (warm after 50 warmups). Also collect CPU/mem metrics and if possible dmesg/syslog for IO issues.
[08:20] Priya: we'll get that data to you.
[08:22] Elena: one more question — you mentioned stricter JSON validation may prevent streaming responses. our app relies on streaming to update UI quickly.
[08:30] Luis: full strict validation generally requires completion, but we support incremental validation checkpoints. The streaming client can receive partial tokens and client-side reassembly can perform incremental checks; the tradeoff is that you might not be able to display a complete valid JSON until the end. There's also a 'soft-mode' JSON where validator marks confidence but doesn't block tokens. That reduces overhead but sacrifices some correctness guarantees.
[08:52] Priya: sounds like we need to pick which correctness guarantees are essential.
[08:56] Maya: exactly. for Fidelity-critical paths keep strict-mode on dedicated nodes; for UI previews use soft-mode.
[09:03] Mark: any quick wins we can try today?
[09:06] Luis: yes — disable proxy for the tool and run the self-contained local plugin, and canonicalize prompts as a config change; both are low-effort. We'll provide the scripts.
[09:15] Maya: I'll drop the links in the follow-up email (redwood-json-mode-tuning.pdf and the microbench script).
[09:21] Priya: great.

[09:24] --- midcall technical deep dive, Luis walks through CSV benchmarks (chat link: short-bench.csv) ---

[12:10] Luis: a detail you might see — when token-level validator is implemented in Python glue it adds a lot of overhead; our C++ integrated validator is much faster. Check your runtime build variant.
[12:24] Elena: we pulled standard image from registry: redwood-runtime:v1.12. could that be the python-glue variant?
[12:30] Luis: possible. we have 'runtime-lite' which includes python hooks for easy plugin dev and 'runtime-pro' which is fully native. We'll check the image hash.
[12:40] Maya: action: I'll validate the runtime image and share recommended tags.

[15:02] Priya: question — what about storage-backed KV cache vs in-memory? we don't have huge RAM headroom.
[15:08] Luis: storage-backed KV (mmap'd) helps not to OOM but introduces page faults when chunks are first accessed; warm workloads ok, but cold shards will see spikes. For tail latency-sensitive endpoints keep critical hot KV in memory. There's a hybrid mode where we pin first N layers in RAM and page others.
[15:27] Mark: could compression help? we have high memory constraints.
[15:30] Luis: we support compressed KV blobs; decompression cost is small but adds CPU. For networks with slow disks you might prefer compression.

[18:02] Elena: any notes on scheduler / batch sizing? we saw p99 rise with more concurrency.
[18:09] Luis: scheduler knobs: max_batch_size, max_batch_latency_ms, and preemption for strict-json routes. Also dedicate fewer concurrency slots per GPU so each request gets faster attention. We'll share recommended baseline values.

[21:00] Priya: ok can you outline the follow-up runs and which of you will own them?
[21:06] Maya: I'll coordinate, Luis will run Redwood-side microbench and produce csv, Crescent will run onprem script and provide results, and we'll reconvene in ~10 days.

[21:18] Mark: one last thing — SSO and audit logs — we may need to bring this into procurement.
[21:23] Maya: noted, I'll include SOC2 docs and audit log config in the follow-up packet.

[21:30] --- brief recap / next steps ---

[21:35] Luis: recap: run microbench (four flavors), canonicalize prompts, localize tool plugin, check runtime image for native validator, try isolating strict-json on dedicated nodes, and test float16 vs int8.
[21:50] Priya: thanks everyone, good session. we'll aim to have data shared by next week.
[21:55] Maya: thanks all — I'll schedule the follow up for 2025-11-18 and send the scripts.
[22:02] Elena: thanks.
[22:05] Meeting ended.
